q: Which statement about values in Python is correct?
options: Every expression reduces to a value, and its data type decides what can be done with it
Only numbers count as values, while text is handled by a separate mechanism in the language
The operator alone decides what type a value has, whatever the value is at that point
Data types matter only when a value is printed, and never when values are combined
why: Every expression reduces to a value, and the type of that value decides which operations make sense for it.

q: Which three data types does chapter 1 work with?
options: Integers, lists and dictionaries
Strings, tuples and booleans
Integers, floating-point numbers and strings
Floats, sets and functions
why: The chapter works with integers, floating-point numbers and strings as its first three data types.

q: How does Python store integers and floating-point numbers?
options: Both exactly, the float just has a decimal point
Both in binary with the same fixed precision
Integers exactly, floats in binary with a fixed precision
Floats exactly, integers as approximate binary values
why: The two look alike in the shell but are stored differently: integers exactly, floats in binary with fixed precision.

q: What is special about a Python integer compared with integers in many other languages?
options: It is limited to 64 bits and wraps around silently when it gets too big
It has unlimited precision, so a huge result stays exact instead of overflowing
It is stored in binary, so large values are rounded to the nearest float
It can only hold values that fit in one machine word, or Python stops
why: A Python integer has unlimited precision, so a very large result is still exact and does not overflow.

q: What does this program print?
options: OverflowError
why: An integer has unlimited precision, so 2 ** 64 is exact and adding 1 keeps every digit.

q: Why is round(0.1 + 0.2, 2) used when a program wants to show 0.3?
options: Python cannot add two decimals exactly, so round does the addition instead of the plus sign
The raw float sum is a binary approximation slightly above 0.3, and round tidies it
The sum is exact, and round only changes how it prints
Floats are stored as text, and round converts the text to a number
why: Floats are stored in binary, so 0.1 + 0.2 is only close to 0.3 and rounding gives the clean value.

q: What does this program print?
options: True True
True False
False True
False False
why: The raw sum is 0.30000000000000004 and so is not equal to 0.3, but after round(..., 2) it is 0.3.

q: A shop program adds prices 0.1 and 0.2 and then tests the sum == 0.3, and the test fails. What is the best explanation?
options: The sum is stored in binary and is not exactly 0.3, so compare a rounded value
Python has a bug in the addition of decimals that only newer releases have fixed
Prices must always be integers, because floats cannot be added together in Python
The == operator is only allowed between strings and integers, never between floats
why: Some decimal fractions have no exact binary form, so the float sum is slightly off, and rounding before comparing avoids the problem.

q: How does chapter 1 treat text compared with numbers?
options: As a value like any other, handled with the same expression rules
As a special case that needs its own kind of statement
As a number in disguise that is stored as its digits
As something that can be printed but never combined
why: Text is a value like any other, and the chapter uses the same expression rules for it as for numbers.

q: What is a string in Python?
options: A whole number written without a decimal point
A number that has a fractional part
A name that stores a value in memory
A sequence of characters written between quotes
why: A string is a sequence of characters between quotes.

q: What does this program print?
options: ababc
ab2c
abbc
abcabc
why: The same operators act on strings with a different meaning: * repeats 'ab' twice and + then joins 'c' to the end.

q: Who decides which operator applies first in an expression?
options: The reader, by the way the expression is spaced
The operator that was typed first, from left to right
The data type of the last value in the expression
The language does, through fixed rules
why: The rules for which operator applies first are fixed by the language, not by the reader.

q: Which list is exactly the seven arithmetic operators of chapter 1?
why: The seven operators are +, -, *, /, //, % and **, evaluated in a documented order.

q: What is the difference between / and // in Python?
options: / divides numbers and // divides strings instead of numbers
/ gives a float quotient, while // gives the whole-number part of the division
// gives the remainder of the division and / gives the whole part
They give the same value, but // prints it without a decimal point
why: Floor division // keeps the whole-number quotient, while / gives the float result of the division.

q: Which order of operators is correct, from the one that binds first to the one that binds last?
options: ** first, then *, /, // and %, then + and -
*, /, // and % first, then **, then + and -
+ and - first, then *, /, // and %, then **
All operators together, from left to right
why: Precedence binds ** first, then *, /, // and %, then + and -, and parentheses override it.

q: What does this program print?
why: Without parentheses 2 ** 2 is 4, 4 * 4 is 16 and 10 - 16 is -6; with parentheses 10 - 4 is 6 and 6 * 4 is 24.

q: Which change makes the expression 8 - 2 * 3 evaluate to 18?
options: Write 8 - (2 * 3), because the product must come first
Write (8 - 2) * 3, because parentheses override the order
Write 8 - 2 * 3 with spaces around the operators
Write 8 - 2 ** 3, because ** binds first
why: Multiplication normally binds before subtraction giving 2, and only parentheses around 8 - 2 override the order to give 6 * 3.

q: What do 23 // 7 and 23 % 7 give together?
options: The whole part 3 and the remainder 2 of the division
The remainder 3 and the whole part 2 of the division
The rounded quotient 3 and the exact quotient 3.28
The float 3.2857 and the integer 23
why: Floor division gives the whole-number quotient and the modulus operator gives the remainder.

q: What does this program print?
why: // gives the whole quotient 3, % gives the remainder 2, and / gives the float 3.2857142857142856.

q: A program must split 47 minutes into whole hours and leftover minutes. Which pair of expressions does it?
options: 47 // 60 for the hours and 47 % 60 for the minutes
47 % 60 for the hours and 47 // 60 for the minutes
47 / 60 for the hours and 47 // 60 for the minutes
47 // 60 for both the hours and the minutes
why: Floor division gives the whole hours, which is 0 here, and the modulus operator gives the leftover 47 minutes.

q: Which two operators work on strings in chapter 1, and what do they do?
options: + repeats a string and * joins two strings
- removes text and / splits text
+ joins two strings and * repeats a string
+ and * both join strings, but * puts a space between them
why: Concatenation joins strings with + and replication repeats a string with *.

q: Why does joining a string to a number with + raise a TypeError?
options: Numbers can never appear in a program that also has strings in it
Python converts the string to a number and then finds that it is not one
The + operator only works on values that have exactly the same length
Python does not convert types silently, so the number must be converted first
why: Python does not convert types silently, so a string and a number cannot be joined until you write str() around the number.

q: What does this program print?
options: TypeError
Alice42
Alice 42
why: Joining a string to a number raises a TypeError because Python does not convert types silently; the except branch prints the class name.

q: Which fix makes 'Total: ' + 3 * 5 work and show Total: 15?
options: str('Total: ' + 3 * 5)
'Total: ' * 3 + 5
'Total: ' + str(3 * 5)
why: 3 * 5 is the integer 15, which must be converted to text before + can join it; wrapping the finished join in str() is too late.

q: What kind of value can be on the right of * when a string is on the left?
options: Another string, which is put after every character
A float, which is rounded to the nearest whole number
Any value, which is first converted to text
An integer, which is the number of repeats
why: Replication repeats a string an integer number of times with *.

q: What does this program print?
options: abab
ababab
ab2.0
TypeError
why: Replication needs an integer count, and 2.0 is a float, so the operation raises a TypeError.

q: What does a binding operation do?
options: It joins two values into one longer value
It converts a value from one type to another
It gives a value a name, so later expressions can use it
It prints a value on the screen
why: Assignment is the operation that gives a value a name so that later expressions can use it.

q: Which statement stores the value 42 in a variable called spam?
options: 42 = spam
spam == 42
spam = 42
store spam 42
why: An assignment statement stores a value in a variable with the = operator, with the name on the left.

q: Which variable name follows the PEP 8 recommendation?
options: TotalPrice
total_price
total-price
TOTAL PRICE
why: PEP 8 recommends lower_case names with underscores for variables.

q: What does this program print?
options: spam + 2
why: The variable is first bound to 40, and the second assignment stores the new value 40 + 2 under the same name.

q: Which six built-in functions does the first program of chapter 1 use?
options: print, input, len, list, int and float
print, open, len, str, int and float
print, input, sum, str, int and round
print, input, len, str, int and float
why: The chapter's six are print, input, len, str, int and float, all available without importing anything.

q: What does it mean that print and len are built-in functions?
options: They must be imported from a module before every use
They are always available, without importing anything
They are only available in the interactive shell
They can only be used inside a function you write
why: Built-in functions are always available in Python without an import.

q: Which pair of functions connects a program to its user?
options: input sends text out and print reads text in
len sends text out and str reads text in
print sends text out and input reads text in
print and input both send text out
why: print sends text out to the user and input reads text in from the user.

q: What does print() do with the value it is given?
options: It stores the value in a variable
It returns the value as a string to the program
It writes the value as text to the screen
It converts the value into an integer
why: print() writes its arguments as text to the screen.

q: What does this program print?
options: Hi 3 + 4
Hi7
Hi 7
Hi 34
why: print writes each argument as text, evaluating 3 + 4 to 7 first, and separates the arguments with a space.

q: What type of value does input() always return?
options: An integer
A float
Whatever type the user typed
A string
why: input() waits for the user to type and always returns a string.

q: A program runs age = input() and then print(age + 1). The user types 41. What happens?
options: A TypeError, because age is the text '41' and 1 is a number
It prints 42, because input() sees that 41 is a number
It prints 411, because + joins the digits
It prints 41, because the +1 is ignored
why: input() always returns a string, so age is '41' and joining a string to a number raises a TypeError.

q: Why do programs need str, int and float so often?
options: Because Python forgets the type of a value after every line
Because input returns text, and values must be converted to the type needed
Because numbers cannot be stored in variables without them
Because print refuses to write integers and floats
why: Since input gives text, programs convert values between types with str, int and float.

q: Why does int('4.2') fail?
options: The text is not a whole number, and int() refuses it with a ValueError
int() rounds 4.2 down to 4 but prints a warning message first
int() can only be used on values that are already numbers in the program
Text with a decimal point is always read as a float and then ignored
why: int() refuses a string that is not a whole number, and it does so with a ValueError.

q: What does this program print?
why: int() turns the texts into numbers so + adds them to 15, while the plain strings are joined into '78'.

q: What does this program print?
options: ValueError
TypeError
why: The text '4.2' is not a whole number, so int() raises a ValueError.

q: Which call turns the number 29 into the text '29'?
options: int(29)
float(29)
len(29)
str(29)
why: str() converts a value to a string, so str(29) gives '29'.

q: How is a measurement function such as len different from a conversion function?
options: It changes the value into a number and hides the original value
It only works on numbers and never on text values in a program
It writes the value on the screen instead of returning it
It reports a property of a value instead of changing its type
why: Measurement functions measure a value rather than convert it, and len is the first the chapter uses.

q: What does len() return for a string?
options: The number of words in it
The value of its last character
The number of characters in it
The number of characters minus one
why: The len function returns the number of characters in a string.

q: What does this program print?
why: len counts every character, including the space, so 'hello world' has 11, and the empty string has 0.

q: Why does the chapter say where code runs matters as much as what it says?
options: Because the same code always gives different answers on every computer you use
Because the Python students run in 2026 is newer than the one the chapter describes
Because Python code cannot run anywhere outside of the interactive shell
Because newer versions delete the built-in functions that older ones had
why: The Python students run is newer than the one the chapter describes, so the environment shapes what they see.

q: Which release is current in the chapter, and which one arrives on 1 October 2026?
options: 3.13 is current and 3.14 arrives
3.15 is current and 3.16 arrives
3.14 is current and 3.15 arrives
3.14 is current and 4.0 arrives

q: How does the interactive environment evaluate what you type?
options: All expressions wait and run together when you close the shell
Each expression is evaluated as soon as it is entered
Only statements run, and expressions must be printed first
Expressions run only after they have been saved in a file
why: In the interactive shell each expression is evaluated as soon as it is entered.

q: Which Python release replaced the interactive shell with a better interactive interpreter?
options: Python 3.13
Python 3.11
Python 3.12
Python 3.15
why: Python 3.13 replaced the interactive shell with a better interactive interpreter and improved its error messages.

q: What changed for a student typing a first expression in the newer interactive interpreter?
options: The interactive interpreter is better and its error messages are improved
Expressions are no longer evaluated until a program is saved
Only the print function can be used in it
It accepts strings but no longer accepts numbers
why: The newer interpreter improved the shell and its error messages, which changes what students see from the first expression.

q: Why does the build of CPython matter to a programmer?
options: The build decides which operators the language has
The build decides how programs can use the machine
The build changes the meaning of every data type
The build is chosen by the program at run time
why: CPython is built in more than one way, and the build decides how programs can use the machine.

q: Since which release does CPython offer an experimental free-threaded build?
options: Python 3.10
Python 3.12
Python 3.14

It replaces the interactive shell that was used before Python 3.13
It previews the course's multithreading outcome, as it can run threads in parallel
It is needed to run any program that uses strings or numbers at all

q: Why does an advanced course teach modern practice next to the book's basics?
options: Because the book's basics no longer work in current versions of Python
Because modern practice replaces the basics of the book completely
So the book's string building and first program are paired with today's tools
Because the basics are only meant for beginners and are skipped here

q: Which statement about building strings is correct?
options: Concatenation works, but f-strings are the idiomatic way to mix text and values
Concatenation is deprecated and raises an error in newer versions of Python
F-strings can only hold plain text, and they can never hold any values
Mixing text and values is only possible with the input function of Python

q: What happens to an expression written inside braces in an f-string?
options: It is evaluated while the string is built
It is kept as text, braces included
It is only allowed to be a variable name
It is evaluated before the whole program starts
why: An f-string evaluates expressions inside braces as it builds the string.

options: PEP 8
PEP 701
PEP 20

options: With how the source code of a program is printed
With how packages and interpreters are installed
With how two strings are joined into one
With how the variables of a program are named
